content: Amidines are a specific class of chemical compounds derived from oxoacids. An oxoacid, in this context, must have the general formula RnE(=O)OH, where R represents a substituent group. In the process of forming an amidine, the hydroxyl group (−OH) of the oxoacid is replaced by an amino group (−NH2), and the oxo group (=O) is replaced by an imino group (=NR). This substitution results in the general structure of amidines being RnE(=NR)NR2. When the parent oxoacid is a carboxylic acid, the resulting amidine is specifically referred to as a carboxamidine. Carboxamidines are characterized by their general structure and are often simply called amidines, as they are the most commonly encountered type of amidine in organic chemistry. The simplest amidine is acetamidine, which has the molecular formula CH3C(=NH)NH2. Other notable examples of amidines include DBU (1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]undec-7-ene) and diminazene, both of which are widely recognized in various chemical and pharmaceutical applications.
